questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1973 rise in the world price of oil occurred
questions.stem: Note 114 asks the translator to explain why the world price of crude oil rose so sharply in 1973 and which factor did most to produce it.

options.text: Because importers had built large stocks, so the sudden rise was a demand surge from replenishing
options.misconception: treats the price rise as a demand surge from stocking

options.text: Because producers had held back output for years and then used their new bargaining power
Because the world had run out of oil, so the rise reflected physical exhaustion of the field
options.misconception: claims physical exhaustion drove the price

options.text: Because a change in shipping technology made oil cheaper to move, raising demand sharply
options.misconception: invents a shipping cause for the price rise

questions.explanation: Producers had limited new supply for years and coordinated output restraint, so the rise reflected a shift in bargaining power. Stocking demand or exhaustion of the field misstates the cause.
questions.hint: Ask who controlled the pace of new supply.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the years after the oil shock
questions.learningObjective: Read post-shock data to identify the shock's fingerprint
questions.stem: Comment 27 shows a table in which growth was eight percent in one economy, two percent in a second and minus four percent in a third, and asks which pattern the module should read as the shock's fingerprint.

options.text: The economy with eight percent growth was hit hardest, because the fastest growth needed the most oil
options.misconception: reads fastest growth as the heaviest hit

options.text: The three rows tell the module nothing, because growth rates cannot reveal an external shock
options.misconception: denies that the comparison carries information

options.text: The economy with two percent growth was hit hardest, because it fell furthest from the others
options.misconception: judges the hit by distance from the leader

options.text: The economy that grew least and fell into decline was the heaviest importer of oil

questions.explanation: The heaviest importers lost most and the exporters of oil kept growing, so a row that fell while others rose marks the shock's fingerprint. Reading growth speed misses the pattern.
questions.hint: Look for the row that moved against the others.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Recycling the oil revenue through the banks
questions.learningObjective: Explain why oil revenue was placed in foreign banks rather than spent at once
questions.stem: Footnote 322 asks why the surplus oil revenue of the exporting states was put into foreign banks rather than spent at once.

options.text: Depositing it abroad recycled the spending, so importing countries had funds to buy the oil
Depositing it abroad was a way of hiding the money from the citizens of the exporting state
options.misconception: gives concealment a role no source supports

options.text: Depositing it abroad was required because the oil could not be stored for long periods
options.misconception: invents a storage requirement that explains the deposits

options.text: Depositing it abroad raised the interest rate paid to the exporters on their revenue
options.misconception: makes the deposit a rate-raising device

questions.explanation: Money placed abroad and later lent abroad became purchasing power for the countries buying oil. Concealment or storage motives are not in the record.
questions.hint: Ask who could spend the money afterwards.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second oil rise and the repricing of debt
questions.learningObjective: Identify who bore the exchange rate risk in a foreign currency loan

stimulus.body: The principal shall be repaid in United States dollars, or in an amount of the borrower's own currency computed at the rate prevailing on the date of each payment. The borrower may not vary the currency of repayment without the written consent of the lender.

questions.stem: Glossary 105 attaches an extract from a loan agreement to the draft and asks what it shows about where the risk sat.

options.text: The extract shows that the loan was protected against every change in the exchange rate
options.misconception: reads the clause as removing all exchange rate risk

options.text: The extract shows that the lender had no rights over the currency of repayment
options.misconception: denies the consent clause in the text

options.text: The extract shows the borrower bearing the exchange rate risk, since repayment was fixed in dollars
The extract shows that the loan could be repaid in any currency the borrower chose
options.misconception: ignores the consent requirement stated in the text

questions.explanation: Because the local-currency amount was computed at the rate on the payment date, a weaker currency meant more was owed. Reading the clause as protection misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask which currency sets the amount owed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why two sectors stayed outside the rules
questions.learningObjective: Explain why informal and farm credit stayed outside the lending rules
questions.stem: Footnote 375 asks for a written explanation of why farm loans and small informal business credit were left outside the new lending rules.

answer.exemplar: The rules were written for banks that took deposits from the public and made loans in formal contracts, and for governments that could be made to answer for their commitments. Most farm credit and much small business credit went through lenders who took deposits informally and lent without registered contracts. Bringing them inside would have required the state to reach into every village shop and lender, and to make a claim on debts that were often recorded only in a notebook.

questions.explanation: A full answer explains the scope of the rules and why the excluded lending was hard to reach. Answers that cite unfairness, or the size of the sector alone, each leave the reach problem out.
questions.hint: Explain what the rules could reach and why.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the last round had to be one package
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the final measures had to be a single package
questions.stem: Note 160 asks the translator to connect the last round of measures to the problems it was meant to solve.

options.text: The package solved the oil problem alone, and the rest of its measures were ceremonial
options.misconception: reduces the package to one of its problems

options.text: The package failed because the oil price was beyond the reach of any set of measures
options.misconception: blames the price rather than the design of the package

options.text: The package worked because the exporters agreed to fund it without conditions
options.misconception: credits exporters with unconditional financing

options.text: The package addressed linked problems, since the oil, the credit and the payments could not be fixed apart

questions.explanation: A synthesis must show the measures as a package because the price, the credit terms and the payments position reinforced one another. Isolating one problem breaks the linkage.
questions.hint: Show the problems as linked, not separate.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why disputes needed a referee both sides obeyed
questions.learningObjective: Identify the source of a disputes mechanism's authority
questions.stem: Redaction 121 asks what made a disputes mechanism credible to the parties who used it.

options.text: Both sides accepted the referee's rulings in advance, before the disputes arose
The referee was chosen by each side separately and the two choices were identical
options.misconception: invents a rule that both sides always chose the same referee

options.text: The referee's rulings were published but carried no obligation to be followed
options.misconception: treats publication as if it created no duty to comply

options.text: The mechanism worked because every party feared the loss of trade with its partners
options.misconception: reads compliance as fear rather than as agreed acceptance

questions.explanation: Credibility came from prior acceptance, so a ruling could be enforced without persuading anyone anew. Publishing or pressuring alone does not make a decision binding.
questions.hint: Ask what was agreed before the first case.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Concentrated gains and diffuse costs
questions.learningObjective: Identify the pattern of concentrated gains and diffuse costs
questions.stem: Redaction 104 shows a table in which one country's gain was concentrated in a single export sector while its import bill was spread across every household, and asks what this shows.

options.text: Both the gain and the cost were concentrated, so the two could be matched easily
options.misconception: claims the cost was as concentrated as the gain

options.text: Both were diffuse, so no group could claim that the shock had helped it
options.misconception: claims the gain was diffuse as well

options.text: The gain was concentrated and the cost was diffuse, so the gains could be defended hard
The table shows nothing about distribution, because it lists only national totals
options.misconception: denies that national totals can show distribution

questions.explanation: Concentrated gains give a well organised group a reason to defend the arrangement, while diffuse costs spread the pain thinly. Calling the cost concentrated misreads the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask how widely each side is spread.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the oil price rise reached the countries that bought oil
questions.stem: Margin 902 flags that the draft says every oil importer was ruined by the 1973 rise and asks for a more careful statement.

options.text: Every importer was ruined, because a higher price always destroys an importing economy
options.misconception: generalises ruin from a severe case

options.text: Importers paid more for every barrel, so the bill grew fastest where oil use was heaviest
Only countries that imported oil were affected, while producers gained nothing from the rise
options.misconception: claims producers gained nothing from the rise

options.text: Importers were unaffected, because oil prices at the time barely moved in the world market
options.misconception: denies any effect on importers

questions.explanation: A higher world price raised the import bill, and the damage scaled with how much a country bought. Saying every importer was ruined replaces the mechanism with a slogan.
questions.hint: Ask how much the country bought.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the years after the oil shock
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about recovery from a delegation report

stimulus.body: Foreign currency earnings recovered by the second year, but the recovery was carried by two commodities while our traditional exports were still below their former level. Our shipyard and our tyre plant were both working below a third of capacity, and no new orders were coming in.

questions.stem: Margin 915 attaches a note from a trade delegation to the draft and asks what it shows about the years after the shock.

options.text: The report shows that the recovery was broad, because earnings rose across the export basket
options.misconception: claims a broad recovery the report denies

options.text: The report shows that industry was fully employed, since no orders were lost
options.misconception: turns the absence of new orders into full employment

options.text: The report shows that the shock was temporary, because earnings recovered by the second year
options.misconception: reads the recovery in earnings as a complete recovery

options.text: The report shows that earnings recovered on a narrow base while industry stayed idle

questions.explanation: The report pairs rising earnings from two commodities with idle factories, which is a narrow recovery. Reading it as broad or complete contradicts the figures.
questions.hint: Compare the earnings line with the factory line.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Recycling the oil revenue through the banks
questions.learningObjective: Explain how deposits abroad turned into spending by other countries
questions.stem: Margin 951 asks for a written explanation of how money deposited in foreign banks by the oil exporters eventually came back as demand for goods.

answer.exemplar: The exporters put their surplus into banks in other countries rather than spending it at once. Those banks then lent the deposits to importers and governments elsewhere, and the borrowers spent the money on goods, on oil among other things, and on services. The exporters' savings were thus spent by others, so the demand for oil and for trade goods kept circulating instead of dying in a pile of idle balances.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains the deposit, the relending and the spending that turned a stored surplus into demand. Stopping at the deposit misses the step that makes it work.
questions.hint: Follow the deposit into the lending and then the spending.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second oil rise and the repricing of debt
questions.learningObjective: Connect the second oil rise to the treatment of older loans
questions.stem: Redaction 121 asks the translator to connect the second oil rise to the way older loans were treated.

options.text: The second rise had no bearing on older loans, because they had been signed at fixed prices
options.misconception: claims old loans were insulated from the new price level

options.text: The second rise cancelled the older loans, because nobody would lend at the old rates
options.misconception: invents a cancellation of older credit

options.text: The second rise raised the cost of servicing older loans in the currencies they were owed
The second rise benefited the borrowers, because higher oil prices meant higher export earnings
options.misconception: shows the rise helping the debtors it harmed

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the new price level to the real burden of servicing credit struck at the old one. Insulating old loans misses the repricing mechanism.
questions.hint: Show how the new price level reached old credit.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why two sectors stayed outside the rules
questions.learningObjective: Identify which sectors the lending rules excluded
questions.stem: Comment 41 asks which two sectors the new lending rules left outside their reach.

options.text: Railways and utilities, because they were owned by foreign companies
options.misconception: names sectors the rules normally covered

options.text: Informal small business lending and much of the farm credit that never passed through a bank
Government bonds and central bank bills, because they were issued inside the country
options.misconception: names instruments that the rules plainly governed

options.text: Export credit and import guarantees, because they involved foreign currencies
options.misconception: names the instruments the rules were designed to govern

questions.explanation: The rules reached formal intermediaries and their contracts, while informal shop credit and farm lending stayed outside. Naming railways or government paper misreads the exclusion.
questions.hint: Ask which lending never passed through a formal bank.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the last round had to be one package
questions.learningObjective: Describe how the components of the final package were presented
questions.stem: Margin 981 shows a table with four components and asks the module to describe how they were presented.

options.text: The components were announced separately, so each could be withdrawn without affecting the others
options.misconception: describes a piecemeal approach the item denies

options.text: The components covered only the lenders, with no measure on the price of oil itself
options.misconception: omits the price component the table records

options.text: The components were voluntary, so the table lists suggestions rather than commitments
options.misconception: recasts commitments as voluntary suggestions

options.text: The components were presented as one set, with changes to one matched by changes in the others

questions.explanation: The table shows four components presented together and matched, so a change in one was offset by another. Describing them as separate or voluntary misreads the framing.
questions.hint: Ask how the parts were matched to each other.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why disputes needed a referee both sides obeyed
questions.learningObjective: Explain where a referee's authority actually came from
questions.stem: Footnote 366 says the draft claims the referee had the power to order whatever it liked, and asks for the corrected account.

options.text: Its power came from the prior commitment to accept its rulings, not from any power of its own
Its power came from the size of the staff it employed to enforce decisions
options.misconception: invents an enforcement staff as the source of authority

options.text: Its power came from the threat of publishing each ruling before it was made
options.misconception: moves the pressure to a moment before the ruling existed

options.text: Its power came from the fact that no other body was permitted to hear the same dispute
options.misconception: assumes exclusivity was the basis of the authority

questions.explanation: The referee had no power of its own; its authority was the standing commitment of the parties to accept its rulings. Staff or exclusivity supply a source it lacked.
questions.hint: Ask where the authority actually came from.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Concentrated gains and diffuse costs
questions.learningObjective: Identify concentrated gains and diffuse costs in a household account

stimulus.body: Our heating oil cost more in the fourth quarter than in any quarter since my father kept the books, and we have cut the number of rooms we use. The company that sells to the state gets paid more than last year, and the men it employs are paid the same as always.

questions.stem: Glossary 91 attaches a household account to the draft and asks what it shows about who gained and who paid.

options.text: The account shows that the whole gain from the higher price passed to the fuel sellers
options.misconception: assumes the entire gain went to the sellers

options.text: The account shows that the sellers made no gain, since the state still paid the old rate
options.misconception: contradicts what the account says the company received

options.text: The account shows a gain concentrated in the sellers and a cost spread thinly across users
The account shows that neither side was better or worse off, since volumes fell
options.misconception: treats a volume fall as making everyone whole

questions.explanation: The note gives the two surviving reasons for holding, incoming payments and daily valuation, and denies the parity and the redemption promise. Reading it otherwise contradicts the words.
questions.hint: Ask who received the extra money and who paid.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the oil price rise reached a household budget
questions.stem: Footnote 310 asks for a short account of how the 1973 oil rise reached a household budget in a country that imported its fuel.

answer.exemplar: The country bought most of its fuel abroad, so the rise in the world price landed first on the import bill, paid in foreign currency it had to earn from exports. Then it moved through the domestic chain of transport, factory and utility costs, which firms passed on as higher prices. Only after those steps did an ordinary household see the effect in what it paid for fuel and food.

questions.explanation: A good answer contrasts speed, conditionality and repayment basis between the two jobs. Listing both purposes alone misses why separation was useful.
questions.hint: Trace the path from the import bill to the shop.

questions.topic: Reading the years after the oil shock
questions.learningObjective: Connect the oil shock to the growth figures of the years that followed
questions.stem: Glossary 64 asks the translator to connect the oil shock to the growth figures of the years that followed.

options.text: The shock ended growth entirely, and every later figure reflects the collapse
options.misconception: collapses the later record into a single collapse

options.text: The shock raised growth, because higher oil receipts funded more spending
options.misconception: shows the shock raising growth for the economies hit

options.text: Growth was unaffected, since the years after the shock were driven by domestic demand
options.misconception: denies any trace of the shock in the record

options.text: The shock shifted growth between economies, so country averages hid the effect

questions.explanation: A synthesis must show the shock exposing the fragility of the rules and the search for flexibility following from that. Reversing the sequence misses the connection.
questions.hint: Show the effect as a difference between economies.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Recycling the oil revenue through the banks
questions.learningObjective: Identify the best description of the recycling arrangement
questions.stem: Provenance 461 asks which description best fits the recycling of oil revenue through foreign banks.

options.text: Exporters' surpluses were deposited abroad and relent, financing demand for goods elsewhere
Exporters' surpluses were spent at home, so foreign banks only held the money they received
options.misconception: says the money was spent at home and never recycled

options.text: Exporters' surpluses were lent to oil importers, so the borrowing countries repaid in oil
options.misconception: makes the lending go to the oil importers by design

options.text: Exporters' surpluses were withdrawn and burnt, to keep the world price from falling again
options.misconception: invents a scheme to destroy the surpluses

questions.explanation: Recycling means surplus savings in one country becoming spendable income in another, which kept trade growing. Spending at home or destroying the surplus describes something else.
questions.hint: Ask where the deposits were eventually spent.

questions.topic: The second oil rise and the repricing of debt
questions.learningObjective: Compare debt service ratios to find the most exposed borrower
questions.stem: Provenance 473 shows a table of debt service ratios of 12, 19, 31 and 44 percent for four borrowers and asks which one the module should mark as most exposed.

options.text: The borrower at twelve percent, because a lower ratio leaves less room for any new borrowing
options.misconception: confuses a low ratio with high exposure

options.text: The borrower at nineteen percent, since it is the second highest in the table
options.misconception: picks the second highest without any stated principle

options.text: The borrower at forty-four percent, because most of its export earnings go on servicing debt
The borrower at thirty-one percent, because a ratio above thirty is always fatal
options.misconception: invents a fixed threshold that marks distress

questions.explanation: Exposure is measured by how much of the export earnings go on servicing debt, so the highest ratio is the heaviest burden. Ranking by list position misreads the table.
questions.hint: Look at the largest share of earnings committed.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the gap between formal and informal credit persisted
questions.stem: Margin 970 says the draft treats the gap between formal and informal credit as a matter of paperwork and asks for the corrected account.

options.text: The gap was clerical, because the forms differed between lenders
options.misconception: reduces the gap to differences in forms

options.text: The gap was reach, because the state could not see or control loans made outside its records
The gap was a shortage of money, since informal lenders had no funds at all
options.misconception: invents a shortage of funds among informal lenders

options.text: The gap was temporary, and the rules would have covered everything by the end of the decade
options.misconception: assumes the gap closed on its own

questions.explanation: The excluded lending was beyond the state's sight and reach, which is why the rules could not apply to it. Calling it clerical or temporary misstates why it persisted.
questions.hint: Ask whether the state could even see the loan.

questions.topic: Why the last round had to be one package
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the agreed text shows about the indivisibility of the package

stimulus.body: The signatories agree that the measures listed in the annex are to be considered as one package. No signatory will implement any part of them separately from the others, and any withdrawal from one element will be treated by the others as a withdrawal from the whole.

questions.stem: Glossary 105 attaches a fragment of the agreed text to the draft and asks what it shows.

options.text: The text shows that each signatory was free to pick whichever measures suited it
options.misconception: contradicts the instruction to act on the package whole

options.text: The text shows that the annex was advisory, and the parties kept their freedom of action
options.misconception: recasts the annex as advisory

options.text: The text shows that the parties had already fallen out over how to divide the burden
options.misconception: invents a dispute the text does not mention

options.text: The text shows that the measures had to move together or be withdrawn together

questions.explanation: The text makes the annex indivisible, with any withdrawal treated as withdrawal from the whole. Reading it as a menu of options or as advisory contradicts the words.
questions.hint: Look at the rule about withdrawing from one part.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why disputes needed a referee both sides obeyed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why parties obeyed rulings they disliked
questions.stem: Glossary 98 asks for a written account of why the parties obeyed a referee's ruling even when they disliked it.

answer.exemplar: They had agreed in advance to accept the ruling, and that agreement was worth more than any one verdict. A party that ignored a decision it disliked would have shown that the whole process was optional, and every later ruling, including the ones that suited it, would have been worth nothing. So the price of refusing was not the cost of the case at hand but the loss of a procedure that the party expected to need again.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that refusing one ruling undermined the value of the procedure for the future. Citing the cost of the case alone leaves out that logic.
questions.hint: Explain the value of the procedure in future.

questions.learningObjective: Connect concentrated gains and diffuse costs to the difficulty of reform

options.text: It made reform easy, because almost everyone paid a small share of a large total

It left reform unchanged, because the pattern was the same as after the first shock

questions.explanation: A synthesis must link the distribution of gains and costs to the organising capacity of each side. Answers that make reform easy for the wrong reason miss the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask who could organise and who could not.

questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: Select the reading that best fits the 1973 oil rise

options.text: It was a temporary shortage that cleared itself once new drilling came on stream
options.misconception: treats the rise as a brief shortage that self-corrected

options.text: It was a structural change in bargaining power, as producers coordinated to hold supply back

options.misconception: explains the price rise through currency weakness alone

options.text: It was a demand boom in the industrialised economies after years of falling use
options.misconception: invents a demand boom that did not occur

questions.explanation: The rise marked producers gaining the ability to hold supply back and act together, which changed who set the price. A temporary shortage or demand boom misplaces the cause.

questions.stem: Redaction 113 shows a table in which the exporter's private bank deposits rose by sixty percent while the importer's imports rose by twenty percent, and asks what the module should read.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why two sectors stayed outside the rules
questions.learningObjective: Explain what leaving the informal sector outside the rules produced
questions.stem: Glossary 105 asks for a full written account of what leaving the informal sector outside the rules did to the economy.

answer.exemplar: Credit that was not on the books could not be watched, taxed or restructured when something went wrong. When a crop failed or a shop closed, the lender absorbed the loss alone, so no institution was built up that could spread risk, and no public register showed how much was owed. The result was that the informal sector kept lending at rates far above the official ones, and borrowers with no formal record found it hard to move into the regulated system at all.

questions.explanation: A good answer traces what the exclusion removed: oversight, the spreading of risk and access to cheaper credit. Mentioning only higher rates leaves out the wider consequences.
questions.hint: Trace what the exclusion removed from the system.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an importer's currency weakened after the 1973 oil rise
questions.stem: Caption 12 asks the translator to explain in writing why an importer's currency weakened after the 1973 oil rise.

answer.exemplar: An importer paid for oil in foreign currency, and the oil bill grew with the world price. To meet a larger bill in the same currency, the country had to sell more exports or raise its own prices to attract more foreign earnings. Either route took purchasing power away from other imports and from households, and a currency that weakened against the oil supplier's currency made the next barrel cost even more.

questions.explanation: An importer paid for oil in foreign currency, and the bill grew with the world price, so more exports or higher prices were needed to pay it. A weaker currency then made the next barrel dearer.
questions.hint: Show the bill, the payment and the feedback.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why disputes needed a referee both sides obeyed
questions.learningObjective: Describe what happens when one party stops complying with rulings
questions.stem: Note 121 asks for a short written account of what happens to a disputes mechanism when one party begins ignoring rulings.

answer.exemplar: A disputes mechanism lives entirely on the expectation that rulings will be accepted. When a party begins ignoring decisions it dislikes, the first effect is not on that case but on every other: the other side now has no reason to accept rulings either, because acceptance buys nothing if refusal is tolerated. The referee may still produce careful findings, but findings that neither side is obliged to follow are records rather than decisions, and the procedure has already stopped working.

questions.explanation: A good answer shows the mechanism failing through the withdrawal of reciprocal acceptance. Focusing on the disobedient party's case misses where the system fails.
questions.hint: Explain what the other side stops doing.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why informal lending persisted after credit was opened up
questions.stem: Comment 76 asks for a written account of why the informality of small business lending persisted even after credit was opened to more borrowers.

answer.exemplar: Official credit arrived in the towns, through banks with branches, staff and paperwork, and it was priced for a risk that a borrower with no recorded business could hardly be judged on. A shopkeeper who had traded for years could show a landlord, a supplier or a customer's word, but none of those counted. The informal lender, who knew the person rather than the papers, could lend against exactly what the applicant had, and the applicant stayed where the credit fitted.

questions.explanation: A good answer shows the mismatch between what official lenders could assess and what small borrowers could offer. Citing cost alone leaves out the assessment problem.

options.misconception: claims the underlying problem disappeared

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the linked design to a change in who bore the cost, with each contribution matched to the other's. Freezing the distribution breaks the connection.
questions.hint: Show how the shares changed and why.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why disputes needed a referee both sides obeyed
questions.learningObjective: Describe the standing of a referee whose rulings both sides obeyed
questions.stem: Caption 29 asks which description the draft should give of the referee's standing.

options.text: A body whose authority rested on the prior commitment of the parties to accept its rulings
A branch of one government, whose rulings that government could at any time overrule
options.misconception: makes the referee an instrument of one government

options.text: A panel of commercial arbitrators appointed anew for every dispute that arose
options.misconception: makes the referee a temporary panel, not a standing body

options.text: An academic tribunal whose findings were published for the parties to consider
options.misconception: reduces the referee's output to published findings

questions.explanation: The referee's standing came from the commitment of the parties before the disputes arose, which made its rulings binding. Making it a branch of a government removes that basis.
questions.hint: Ask where the binding force came from.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Concentrated gains and diffuse costs
questions.learningObjective: Read a burden table to judge how the cost was distributed
questions.stem: Glossary 105 shows a table in which the lowest income group pays 9 percent of the burden, the next 12, then 15, 18 and 21, and asks what the module should read.

options.text: The burden was regressive, because the lowest group paid a larger share than the richest
options.misconception: reads the shares in the wrong direction

options.text: The burden was even, because every group paid within a few points of the others
options.misconception: treats a twelve point spread as an even distribution

options.text: The burden was progressive in cash terms, since higher shares fell on the better off
The table shows nothing about distribution, because it gives no absolute figures
options.misconception: denies that shares can show distribution

questions.explanation: A larger share of the burden on higher income groups shows the charge falling harder on the better off. Calling it regressive or even misreads the spread.
questions.hint: Ask which end of the table carries more.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain the 1973 oil rise as a transfer of income
questions.stem: Comment 76 says the draft argues the 1973 rise was a disaster for everyone and asks the translator to correct it.

options.text: It was a disaster for everyone, because any increase in a basic input hurts every economy
options.misconception: assumes a universal effect from a shared input

options.text: It was a transfer, moving income from oil buyers to oil sellers while disrupting plans
It was a disaster for producers, because they could no longer sell the extra output they had
options.misconception: invents unsold output that the rise created

options.text: It changed nothing, because oil was a small part of every country's spending
options.misconception: denies any effect from a shared input

questions.explanation: A price rise in a traded input transfers income between its buyers and sellers while it disrupts plans set at the old price. Calling it a universal disaster misses the transfer.
questions.hint: Ask whose income the price moved.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the years after the oil shock
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about the years after the shock from a budget statement

stimulus.body: Our revenue from the oil companies' taxes has risen, but the cost of subsidising fuel for domestic transport and for the farms has risen further. The deficit for the year is larger than the one before, and it will be financed by borrowing from abroad.

questions.stem: Caption 29 attaches a budget statement to the draft and asks what it shows about the years after the shock.

options.text: The statement shows the shock had been fully absorbed, since revenue rose and no borrowing followed
options.misconception: claims the deficit was covered without borrowing

options.text: The statement shows the government chose not to respond, since tax rates never appear in it
options.misconception: treats silence about tax rates as deliberate inaction

options.text: The statement shows the problem was fiscal only, and the external position was unaffected
options.misconception: denies any external effect

options.text: The statement shows higher revenues eaten by subsidies and by the cost of foreign borrowing

questions.explanation: The statement shows new revenue from the oil trade offset by a larger fuel subsidy and by foreign borrowing. Reading it as full absorption contradicts the figures.
questions.hint: Track the revenues against the subsidies.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Recycling the oil revenue through the banks
questions.learningObjective: Explain what followed when the flow of deposits slowed
questions.stem: Caption 60 asks for a written account of what happened when the oil exporters began to deposit less of their revenue abroad.

answer.exemplar: The recycling depended on a flow. When the exporters slowed the pace of their deposits, the loans that had been made abroad could not be replaced at the same speed, so the lenders had to find new borrowers or call in what they had lent. Some borrowers could not meet the calls, credit tightened for the countries that depended on it, and the damage reached far beyond the oil trade itself.

questions.explanation: A full answer explains the dependence on a continuing flow and traces the effect of its slowdown through lending and credit. Stopping at the oil market misses how widely the effect ran.
questions.hint: Trace what happens to the loans already made.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second oil rise and the repricing of debt
questions.learningObjective: Connect the second oil rise to the shift in what lenders demanded
questions.stem: Redaction 139 asks the translator to connect the second oil rise to the shift in what lenders demanded from borrowers.

options.text: The rise made lenders withdraw from lending entirely, which was the only visible change
options.misconception: claims lenders simply stopped lending

options.text: The rise made lenders charge the same rates but demand longer periods of grace
options.misconception: invents an unchanged price with changed terms

options.text: The rise made lenders price the risk of currency and oil exposure into new terms
The rise had no effect on lending, because the terms of credit were never linked to oil
options.misconception: denies any connection between the shock and credit terms

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the shock to a repricing of perceived risk in the terms lenders set. A retreat from lending or an unchanged price breaks the argument.
questions.hint: Show how the shock entered the contracts.
